utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In fact, each of the categories for Muslims, Croats, Serbs, and the other category, none of the numbers actually match. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not perfectly, don't match, of course. But the differences are small.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would that be considered a margin of error or how would you describe those differences?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe these are marginal differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The category that you have in your table 2 on page 7 of your report, namely, "other," you have an asterisk by that, and you identify that as Yugoslavs only.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you, Doctor, in connection with formulating the conclusions that you did in this report, verify or try to determine from the 1991 census what the composition was of those individuals who identified themselves in the survey as Yugoslavs; namely, did you further, in order to make your report more reliable and accurate, determine which ethnic group of the three these Yugoslavs were actually members of?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is impossible using the census data. Once someone reported the ethnicity "Yugoslav," that's the ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you, Doctor, make any assumptions as to whether or not the individuals that identified themselves as Yugoslavs belonged to one or a different ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't make any assumptions about ethnicity of those reported as Yugoslavs, any other ethnicity. I just used the reported ethnicity from the census.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What per cent as a whole, if you can share with me, is this other category?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslavs together with the other ethnic group. On the next page, page 8, table 3, English translation of the report, the "others" are 8.3 per cent in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, help me understand this margin of error, if you will, or my understanding of margin of error. If we can establish that a hundred per cent of this other category that we've identified as the Yugoslavs were actually - and we know that's not realistic, it's a hypothetical question - were actually of the ethnic makeup Serb, would you agree with me then that the -- at the very least, the margin of error of your report and data would be that 8.3 per cent?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 8.3 per cent would be then classified mistakenly as "others" while, in fact, they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, during your direct testimony, on page 45, specifically lines 6 through 10, you gave us a somewhat example, if you will, of census classifications. And if I may read that portion of it, you continued in your answer, although it's quite extensive and lengthy, you state on page 6: "And we know examples from the Former Yugoslavia that when political situation was more unstable, more people reported themselves as Yugoslavs, just generally as Yugoslavs, and less people reported themselves specifically as Serbs or Muslim or Croats." On line 10 of page 45.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So do you think the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, from what you know, in 1992 was more or less stable?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was certainly less stable than, say, ten years earlier in the Former Yugoslavia or in other countries at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So based on -- so based on your understanding or the assumptions that you make, as you've just told us, that in fact wouldn't it be more realistic in 1991 that there would be, since there was instability or there was an unstable situation, politically speaking, in the Former Yugoslavia, specifically in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that more people would identify themselves as Yugoslavs as opposed to only 8.3 per cent of the population?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I just interrupt. In addition, it would be only fair to ask whether, Witness, if there is any factual basis for the witness to answer this question, the situation in 1981 indicating that "others" as 13 per cent would have been more unstable than in 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is very straightforward conclusion if we understand this figure as a measure of political stability, but I believe it is a very imperfect measure of political instability in a country.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I could direct your attention to page 7 of your report, you identify that the -- on a footnote there below, under "sources," that the 1993 census from Republika Srpska is both methodologically and qualitatively not known, correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Isn't it fair also to state, Doctor, based upon a reasonable degree of scientific statistical and demographic certainty, that indeed reliance upon unknown methodology and quality would only increase the margin of error with respect to the conclusions that one would reach while analysing two different sources?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally, it is. But we should remember that we have the choice between showing some figures that were produced in addition by the local authorities in charge, say, of this area, and using nothing. So it is a choice, a very difficult choice, and we have chosen to show these figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We spoke briefly about immigration and migration of populations. Would you agree with me that in some situations, namely, in the Former Yugoslavia of Bosnia and Herzegovina, from 1995 through 1997, which is specifically the area of focus in your April 19th, 2001 report, that there were factors, politically speaking, such as those that you discussed yesterday, namely, the Dayton Peace Accords, which influenced the exodus of various ethnic groups and populations from one area to another?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, there were certain political factors regulating or influencing population movements in this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And in fact, those were factors that were legally, as best as you can tell us, widely and internationally accepted and quite frankly mandated, were they not?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe this is not a question for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The question is too vague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we can turn back to S228A, please, on page 7. Specifically, Doctor, I'm focussing your attention to subcategory B of paragraph 9, which covers the Prijedor area. There they seem to have a 1995 identification of approximate numbers of each ethnic group. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you, Doctor, do any independent verification to determine the accuracy of what, (a) the term "approximation" means, and (b) whether or not these statistics were in any way manipulated by the people who were formulating these statistics for political reasons?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, accuracy can be assessed by comparing these figures with the figures we produced using the voters' register from 1997. The relative measures, fractions, percentages, can be compared, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what was the conclusion once that comparative analysis was done?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is next page in my report, page number 8, table 3, where the 1995 figures and 1997 figures are shown next to each other. You see that there are certain similarities in the pattern obtained from each of these two sources. There are also certain differences as well. And regarding the second part of your question, manipulation, of course, is beyond my ability, I think, to check. I couldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So with respect to table number 3, Doctor, is it fair that the data that you inputted in order to compile and reach the conclusions that you did in your report, under the subcategory 1995, was directly taken from this source, S228A?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe so. These are the same figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, just help me if you may, just to have an understanding of another table that I didn't quite understand, and that is table 4. I just want to -- my question will be limited because I'm sure we're going to have an opportunity, once you conclude the z-test and the calculations that are not available at this time which appears on page 17 of the April 19th, 2001 report. Just so I can have a better appreciation and understanding of this report, Doctor, is it fair to say that this table is actually distortive, flawed and inaccurate, because it does not include simple things such as the educational status of women or persons from the ages of 16 through 24?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a table that is made only for men age 25 or more years, and it was meant to be only for men of these ages. And the reason was the sample size didn't make sense to analyse women who went missing or died because the numbers were insignificant. So the analysis presented in this table is only presented for men, and the age restriction is related to the fact that we wanted to include only those who completed already their education.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What is the basis to determine that people, whether they are men or women, would not complete higher education, including postgraduate work, at the age of 23 or 24?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: This is beyond the scope of the direct examination and the parts of the report that we were dealing with this week with the witness's testimony. This is part of the report that would be updated with possibly new information. So I think we would be repeating the examination at a subsequent time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In addition to that, please recall what I said earlier on the relevance of education. And therefore, sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor Tabeau, at this time, I just want to thank you for answering my questions and for helping me understand the scientific statistical demography and hopefully, once we get the report, we can have a discussion with respect to your conclusion. Thank you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: However, for the record I have not yet obtained a copy of the questionnaire. So I would just like, for the record, reserve the right to further ask Dr. Tabeau about the questionnaire, if allowed, at a later time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may say something, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I provided four copies of the census questionnaire Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French English transcripts to the registrar. So I hope this can be arranged immediately that you will receive a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, please, via the usher, distribute the pieces. Probably we may come back to this later. I have only three questions, not sophisticated at all, with necessary skepticism admitted vis-a-vis statistics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Nevertheless, do you have any concrete data as regards the census of 1991 which is a discrepancy between the questionnaires sent out and coming back?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that this is a question related to the nonresponse rate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I unfortunately cannot show specific figures. I'm sorry. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Second, we have the figures on the voters' register. Do you have any figures how many persons actually participated in the voting procedure?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have these figures for the whole country, and also for each municipality. Approximately, for the whole country, a number of 2 million, 2.4 million individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What is this in percentage?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Prijedor population of Bosnia-Herzegovina was 4.4 million, approximately, so it is more than 50 per cent of the population, pre-war population, that participated, registered to vote in the election.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And you can compare population and people participating in the election? Correct me if I am wrong, only people over the age of -- including the age of 18 have the right to vote.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this would bring us to a figure of less than 4 million people having the right to vote. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. This percentage I mentioned would be then higher. I don't have it right now ready for you. But it will be certainly more than 50 per cent then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you be so kind and provide us with these figures when you come for another hearing here.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Finally, we were provided with a clip of Kozarski Vjesnik, and it's still open that we ask for the original of this document indicating that it's really from the 2nd of July, 1993. I think we have to come back to this. Did you include this unofficial census results in any of your reports?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other reports?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In your own report or in the upcoming report.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The original document, Your Honour? That's the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The question is whether or not you included in your report --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- presented here, or is it your intention to include these additional figures in another report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can include the Kozarski Vjesnik, the copy that was distributed already yesterday, but I understand that this copy is already in possession of everyone. So my intention is not to include once again a document which is available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This is my question. It's an additional information to that what you provided in your report. And finally --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the witness misunderstood the question. It is included in the report under the 1993 figures. That is the source, although the report clearly indicates that Dr. Tabeau had no way to verify the methodology or accuracy of the data but simply reported this is what the Serbian authorities reported in 1993 as the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To be quite concrete, a distinction must be made between that what we can read in Kozarski Vjesnik and as we can read there that the official results will be published by the republican bureau of statistics. Did you rely on the official results or on this report in Kozarski Vjesnik?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will discuss this issue with Helge Brunborg, who was doing this part of the report, and clarify with him which exactly of the two sources were used for our figures in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Additional questions? Judge Vassylenko, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Just one question. In this information published in Kozarski Vjesnik, there is a very interesting figure that 96.3 per cent of the population of Prijedor have Serbian citizenship. And I would like to know whether you have information about the citizenship of the population of Republika Srpska, how many persons living in Republika Srpska now have Serbian citizenship?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have this information right now in my office, especially not for the period 1993 or 1995. I can explore, investigate the issue, and report later on the result of this investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any further questions by one of the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I have a very brief question, just to clarify something in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is it correct, Doctor, that all of the breakdowns of ethnicities in the 1991 census was done by self-classification? If a person reported themselves as a Yugoslav, they were classified as a Yugoslav. If they reported themselves as a Croat, they were recorded as a Croat. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. Only considering and analysing as, for instance, Serbs reported themselves as Serb ethnicity, we considered only them as Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Again, in the data used in 1997, because voters did not report their ethnicity but you determined that by linking the voter to the 1991 census, it was again self-classification as to what a person felt themselves to be, what ethnicity. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. It is important because in this case, we used still one, the same definition of ethnicity, and compare population, the population, in two different periods of time. Consistent definition of ethnicity in this way was obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And is it correct that your field is demographics and you are not a professional historian on Yugoslavia, although you mentioned the fact of instability, the various political events influencing how a person would classify themselves is not an area of your specialty?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. I have a common knowledge of history and a limited knowledge of politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, my only other question is given that only a small portion of this report was actually covered in direct examination, I don't know if Your Honour wants us to mark the entire report as an exhibit or how Your Honours, Defence counsel, wish to handle that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I first hear observations by the Defence as regards the admissibility of this tendered report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we can mark it, as a suggestion, provisionally, and then wait until the final report is included or given to us, and then the doctor can decide if she wants to make it as an annex to her report or if the same data and information will be relied upon and subject to that second report. I would prefer that we wait for the second report so that it would be complete. However, acceptable also to accepting this report as an exhibit and have no objection to the report to be produced or marked as an exhibit and introduced into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The next available number will be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be S230, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then the entire report will be admitted into evidence as S230.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just for the record, I believe the -- aside from portions of the report discussing the sources and methodology, the actual results that were covered in the testimony relate to pages 7 through 10 of this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Additional questions by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps -- I'm sorry. Does Your Honour want the questionnaire or does either the Defence or Your Honours want the questionnaire marked as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I just wanted to turn to this question when turning to the Defence. Do you have any additional questions based on this questionnaire?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Quite frankly, Your Honour, I haven't had time to digest the questionnaire in full length, but I do have, if permitted by the Court to ask a follow-up question in the area covered by re-direct

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: sure the area of self-classification will be raised at a later time as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think, to avoid repetitious, we should do it when we have the entire and updated report before us. Then I can see no additional questions. Thank you very much, Madam Tabeau, for providing us with this information. And we are looking forward to have as soon as possible the documents and, as mentioned, it would be favourable to have this before the Court recess.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the usher please escort Madam Tabeau out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we hear immediately the next witness and may be escorted into the courtroom immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Hopefully the witness is outside, Mr. O'Donnell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Not to forget that I think it's without doubt, this document, the questionnaire, will be admitted into evidence as S231B, as evidently we don't have an English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just a reminder to Your Honour, I don't know if you want to mark it, but the report also has a French version, if you wanted to give that a different number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we did it always with a C. Right? Then please do so. Maybe in order to use all the available time ask the -- well, the witness appears already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. O'Donnell, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for coming immediately. May we please hear, first, your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please, be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the floor is for the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, would you state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: My full name is Bernard Patrick O'Donnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. O'Donnell, who are you employed by?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I'm employed by the Office of the Prosecutor as an investigations team leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How long have you worked for the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Since 1996, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Prior to joining the Office of the Prosecutor, did you have any experience in law enforcement?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I joined the Australian federal police about 20 years ago and worked with the federal police until the year 2000, and was on leave without pay whilst attached to the Tribunal up until that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. O'Donnell, on the 23rd of March of 2001, can you tell us what -- where you went and your duties for the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: On the 23rd of March, 2001, Your Honours, I undertook the formal arrest of Mr. Stakic in Belgrade on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor, and brought Mr. Stakic back to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: To clarify the matter, did you go and detain Mr. Stakic in Belgrade or was he already detained by authorities there?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Stakic had already been detained by local authorities in Belgrade. He was handed over to me at the airport in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Prior to testifying about -- I'm going to question you about the arrest. Have you refreshed your recollection with any notes that you took at that time?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, I have. The arrest procedure and the reading of rights was tape recorded, Your Honours. I prepared a transcript of that tape recording, and that was lodged into evidence. Before giving evidence, I refreshed my memory from those notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see Dr. Stakic in court today?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just for the record, where is he sitting?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Stakic is sitting against the wall beside the security officer, wearing a grey suit and a maroon tie with dots.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. O'Donnell, do you have your notes with you?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If you need to refer to your notes, just indicate to me prior to doing so that you are doing that. Tell us what happened when you arrived in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: When I arrived in Belgrade, I met with local authorities, obtained the details of those people, identified myself to the local authorities, made arrangements for Mr. Stakic to be brought to the aircraft. I advised local authorities that I wanted to undertake the reading of the rights as soon as possible. That was done on the aircraft, and we departed for The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And you mentioned a tape recording. When did you begin to tape record your interactions with the detained individual, Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: From the first words that I said to Mr. Stakic, the tape recorder was on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Where was it that you actually met him for the first time?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I first met him on the aircraft. He was transferred onto the aircraft, but not by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So you saw him being transferred onto the aircraft but first spoke to him on the aircraft. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And you indicated that you prepared a transcript of a tape that you made of that conversation. And was the tape itself also booked into evidence?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, it was, your Honours, both the actual tape recording, the cassette, and the transcript of the cassette recording were lodged into evidence by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have that, and I leave it to Your Honours and Defence counsel's discretion whether you wish the tape played or simply the transcript prepared by Mr. O'Donnell to be read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's come to this later when we discuss the admission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. O'Donnell, you indicated you prepared a transcript. Did you actually do that by listening to the tape and attempting to put down word for word the English translations of your conversation?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you speak Serbian yourself?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Apart from a few words, Your Honours, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And were you using the services of an interpreter employed by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you -- would the best and most accurate testimony regarding that conversation be if you read the transcript that you prepared?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, it would. I transcribed the tape myself, and it is an accurate transcription of what is contained on the audiocassette.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could you then read the transcript of your conversations with Mr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: From the notes, I have some preliminary details recorded of what I've just outlined. "At 5.20 p.m., Mr. Stakic was taken to the aircraft by Serbian security officers. Mr. Stakic was searched for security reasons. Mr. Stakic was wearing blue checked shirt, blue jeans, gold watch with brown strap, black boots, no physical signs of injury. O'Donnell speaks to Mr. Stakic with the assistance of a language assistant." I said: "Dobar Dan, Mr. Stakic." Mr. Stakic said: "Dobar Dan." I said: "My name is Bernard O'Donnell. I'm an investigations team leader with the Office of the Prosecutor at the International Criminal Tribunal in The Hague. This is (redacted), who is my interpreter. I want to tell you firstly that our conversations being audiotape recorded as we speak. Do you understand?" Mr. Stakic said: "Up to now, I understand." I said: "Can I have your full name, please?" He said: "Milomir Stakic." I said: "Your date of birth?" He said: "19 January, 1962." I said: "Your father's name?" He said: "Milan." I said: "Where were you born?" He said: "In the village of Mariska, in the municipality of Prijedor." I said: "I'm going to advise you of certain rights that you have. We have an interpreter who is present," indicating (redacted) from Belgrade. "Is it okay with you if the interpreter is present from the Republic of Serbia"? The interpreter introduced herself to Mr. Stakic in Serbian. Mr. Stakic said: "I don't mind." I said to the interpreter, for the purpose of identification -- sorry for the purpose of voice identification: "Can I have your full name, please." And the interpreter said: (redacted) I said: "Do you understand what I am saying to you through the interpreter" to Mr. Stakic. He said: "Up to now, I understand." I said: "I'm going to advise you of certain rights, and I would ask that you listen carefully to what I am telling you. Firstly, you are entitled to be advised of your rights in a language that you understand, as we are doing now, and to the use of an interpreter. Do you understand?" Mr. Stakic nodded. I said: "Can you give me a verbal response, please." He said: "I understand." I said: "I have to advise you that you do not have to say anything. Anything that you do say will be recorded and may be used in evidence in any Tribunal proceedings, including at trial. Do you understand?" Mr. Stakic said: "I understand." I said: "You have the right to be assisted by a legal officer of your choice. Do you understand?" He said: "Yes." I said: "If you cannot afford to hire a lawyer, a legal representative will be appointed for you. Do you understand?" He said: "I understand." I said: "Do you have a legal representative?" He said: "No, I have been arrested. I have no idea. I have been captured." I said: "Do you wish to have a legal advisor appointed for you?" He said: "Yes." I said: "Okay. A legal representative will be arranged for you as soon as possible. Before then, I will continue to advise you of your rights. However, I will again remind you that you do not have to say anything unless you wish to do so." I said: "I have a warrant for your arrest which has been signed by Judge Bennouna of the ICTY, dated January 2001. I now show you that warrant." B/C/S translation of arrest warrant was handed to Mr. Stakic. And I said: "This is a translation of the warrant for your arrest." He said: "Can I read this now?" I said: "I will leave it with you and you can read it now. I will also give you a copy of several rulings from the Tribunal." Rule 21, the B/C/S copy was handed to Mr. Stakic. Rule 42, again, the B/C/S version was handed to Mr. Stakic. And Rule 43, B/C/S version handed to Mr. Stakic. "These Rules explain in more detail your rights as I have given you a summary of now. Mr. Stakic, are you the person named in the warrant that I have handed to you?" Mr. Stakic said: "It is my first name and my last name, so I assume." I said: "I am satisfied that you are the person named in the warrant of arrest. Therefore, I am placing you under arrest on behalf of the Tribunal. You will be transported from here to The Hague in the Netherlands. Once you are in The Hague, you will be given a full copy of the indictment and other paperwork which accompanies the indictment, and you will be served with other documentation. Whilst you will be given a full copy of the indictment once we get to The Hague, I want to tell you very quickly what the indictment is. "Very briefly, the indictment is for the crime of genocide. The brief details are that between the 30th of April, 1992 and the 31st of December, 1992, you, in company with others, planned, instigated, and ordered the establishment of detention facilities at Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje, and the detention there of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats from the municipality of Prijedor under conditions calculated to bring about the physical destruction of the detainees, with the intent to destroy part of the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat groups as such. "It is further alleged that you, and others, had reason to know that people who staffed the detention facilities were killing or causing serious physical or mental harm to Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats with the intent to destroy them, in part, as a national, ethnic or religious group, or that they had done so and you failed to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent such acts." At that stage, there was a knock on the door, and local authorities asked for (redacted) She said: "They called me. I think I have seen enough." I said: "Okay, I will be finished in maybe 2 minutes. It is up to you, you are welcome to stay or go. (redacted) said: "I will see if they need me. Thank you very much." And she left the aircraft. I then returned to speak to go Mr. Stakic and said -- or continued rather, "that you failed to prevent or to punish the perpetrators. That is a brief summary of the charges against you. And as I said, the full details will be served on you when we are back in The Hague. Is there anything that you wish to say at this point?" He said: "No." I said: "Do you wish to ask any questions?" Mr. Stakic said: "I would like to thank you for this brief information and would like to say nothing until I have a legal representative." I said: "Okay. Do you wish to comment on the way that you have been treated so far?" Mr. Stakic said: "I did not know is that there was an indictment against me. I was arrested and now I am slowly trying to get it clear in my head." I said: "Do you have any complaints about the way that we have treated you?" Mr. Stakic said: "You mean here? You? No, absolutely not. I said: "Are you on any medication that you need to take this afternoon?" He said: "I think I have them in my bag here." I said: "When do you need to take them?" He said: "I am taking antibiotics now. I'm only taking painkillers every now and then, when necessary, for my gallstones." I said: "Will you inform us before we get back to The Hague if you need to take any medication?" He said: "Okay." I said: "The time is now 20 minutes to 6.00. We will not have any further conversation until you have a legal officer appointed. If you have any questions, though, please feel free to ask. Mr. Stakic said: "Nothing for now. Thank you." At 5.40 p.m. the conversation was concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. If I could stop now, it just occurs to me it might be more cautious, a better idea, to redact the name of the local interpreter from the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then please redact the name of this person from the transcript, and we'll take this document later under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And I would ask that if counsel or the Court have any need to discuss the names of the local officials dealt with, that that also obviously be in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. O'Donnell, you mentioned a black bag so far in going through the tape.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you discuss, tell us, about that bag.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Stakic had a small black bag with him containing personal documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you -- can you describe it a little bit further? Was it like a briefcase, smaller than a briefcase?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Smaller than a briefcase, from memory, Your Honours. Something of a bag that you would carry in your hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you continue, then, with the conversation that you had. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French English transcripts

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: At 5.40 p.m., we took off from Belgrade. I undertook a search of the bag of Mr. Stakic. I said: "Mr. Stakic, the bag that you have with you, I will search in your presence now so that I can give it back to you and you will have your medication with you. Again, because you don't have a legal officer, I will again caution you that you do not have to say anything unless you want to. Do you understand?" Mr. Stakic said: "Yes." The bag was then searched by myself. It was a small black bag containing identification, paperwork, et cetera, in the name of Milomir Stakic. Mr. Stakic was not restrained during the flight, apart from a seat belt. No conversation regarding the charges on the flight. I said to Mr. Stakic: "When you get to the Tribunal, I suggest that you give the details of your medical condition, and a medical practitioner will be arranged for you as soon as possible." Mr. Stakic said: "I have a certificate from a doctor and some ultrasounds." Mr. Stakic's bag was returned to him so that he would have his medication with him during the flight. I said: "Mr. Stakic, where were you arrested?" He said: "In front of my apartment where I am living for the time being in Belgrade." Sorry: "Where I am living for the time being." I said: "In Belgrade?" He said: "Yes." I said: "When was that?" He said: "Yesterday at about 16.30." At 6.10 that conversation was concluded. At 8.35 p.m., we arrived in the Netherlands. I said: "Mr. Stakic, I just want to inform you of what is happening. Before I do, I have to again caution you that you do not have to say anything, and anything you say can be used in evidence. Do you understand?" He said: "I understand." I said: "Once we stop, we will be met by security staff. That's where we leave you, and the security staff will take you to the Detention Unit. Staff at the Detention Unit will explain to you what is going to happen from there. They will also arrange for you to have legal representation as soon as possible and medical care. Would you please inform the staff at the unit of your medical condition." Mr. Stakic said: "Can I take my medical tests with me?" I said: "Sure." Mr. Stakic then took the paperwork from his bag. At 8.37 p.m., I said: "Do you have the medical documentation that you need from your bag?" He said: "Yes." I said: "Do you have any questions?" Mr. Stakic said: "Will I have an interpreter as well in the other place?" I said: "Yes, you will." At 8.38 p.m. the conversation was concluded and Mr. Stakic was handed over to Dutch security police, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr O'Donnell, referring back to page number 3, you indicated that you asked, about the fifth line or the sixth line from the bottom, that you asked Dr. Stakic if he needed to take any medication this afternoon. And he indicated, "I think I have them in my bag here." And then on the very last page, you indicate that Dr. Stakic took paperwork from his bag regarding the medical tests. This is actually the last line of page 4, he asked: "Can I take my medical tests with me." You said: "Yes," and he took documentation from his bag. On both of these occasions, are you referring to the black bag? Did you understand him to be talking about the black bag that you described earlier?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. He was referring to the black bag in his possession at that time, and took the documents from that black bag.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did he have only one bag with him at the time?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that you had searched the bag and had -- prior to him taking the medication, and that inside the bag there was paperwork and identification with his name on it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Now, after he took the tests, medical tests, from the bag, what did you do with the paperwork and other items of identification in the bag?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I retained possession of the black bag with the other paperwork and brought that back to the Tribunal. Copies of the paperwork were made by myself, photocopies of the paperwork. Copies of that documentation was lodged into evidence. I did the evidence registration and lodged the documentation with the Evidence Unit myself. Copies of -- photocopies of that material were given to the investigation team leader of Team 1. And the actual bag containing the paperwork was also given to the investigations team leader of Team 1, Mr. Inayat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I just ask, you spoke about the evidence registration. Did you add already at that time registration numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time that I handed the documents over to the Evidence Unit, it had an -- what we call an if number, the number for the form that I used to register the evidence. I don't physically assign the numbers myself. That is then done by the Evidence Unit. But following the assignment of the numbers, that range of evidence registration numbers is put on to the IIF form, it appears at the top of the IIF form, linked to those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So just to be clear, the items that you gave to the Evidence Unit regarding the paperwork were actually photocopies, is that correct, that you made of the paperwork that was in the black bag?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The ERN number or evidence record number, I believe it stands for, is a unique number given by the Evidence Unit to each page of documentation that they retain or an item of physical evidence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recall how many, or do you have a record, of how many pages, photocopied pages, you gave to the evidence unit?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, I do. At the time that I handed over the documents to the Evidence Unit, I recorded the number of pages. It's a mandatory field in the IIF registration form. There were 81 photocopied pages. That was then assigned the ERN range of 0201-7189 to 0201-7269 inclusive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. O'Donnell, can you explain that -- once the range is given, does that necessarily mean that the items are actually stamped, each page, with that number, or is that a separate procedure?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: The photocopies that were handed over to the Evidence Unit are stamped -- each page of documents handed over to the Evidence Unit is stamped physically, and then those numbers are then put on to the IIF form electronically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You are not the person that puts the numbers on the documents, is that correct, and the photocopies you would have given to the evidence unit would not have had the stamped ERN number, correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The documents that you had photocopied, the pages, and for the purposes of my examination, I will now call them originals, although using that definition, the papers that were actually in the black bag, those did not have any stamp put on them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I just interrupt, sorry for this. But this IIF registration form, do you still have this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it possible to provide us and the parties with this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I always heard that there was no reason not to, but I don't understand what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. O'Donnell, is it possible to provide that to the Court?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I have a copy here, Your Honours. To be honest, it's not a decision of mine as to whether it's a provided or not. It's a policy decision. I'm currently unaware of the policy as to whether IIF forms are provided to the Court or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If I could just see the form, please. Your Honour, we would make copies and make this available to the Court. I don't know if Your Honour wants to see it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If the usher, please, could present it to the Defence first, and then to the Judges. It's just for a better understanding to avoid that you have to come back once again, we should make the dishwash today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And perhaps I could ask the registrar, while the Defence is looking at that, to prepare S220 to S226 to be shown to the witness. May I proceed? Do Your Honours need more time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Not to confuse, we should first give an exhibit number to the notes of arrest. Objections? No? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No objection to having the typewritten transcript from the interview marked as an exhibit. We would like also, if Mr. O'Donnell has the handwritten notes, to be made available to us as well, and perhaps we can make that as a separate exhibit if any such notes exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Our understanding is that the OTP, and we are grateful for this, provided two copies of the tape. This would be, then, the document in writing, the notes of arrest, would be S231A. And it should, in addition, it should be registered that the translation can be found on today's transcript, page 68 following. And then this document, which will be provided for us in photocopy, we just saw, will be Document S232. The tapes should go under the number S231-D, that's Detention Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that the tapes be sealed because they will contain the name that we struck from the record earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the same is true for the notes of arrest, also under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And I would actually ask if we could, just as a matter of caution, I'd like to black out the names listed at 4.05 and provide the Court with another copy of this for the Evidence Unit without the names of those local officials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can't see any objections. We will proceed this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. I'm sorry for interrupting you, but I think that we gave number S231 to the questionnaire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the registry please assist.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I did not understand that we marked the questionnaire or that we admitted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's clarify this during the procedure. Please proceed with your line of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. O'Donnell, in answer to Mr. Ostojic's request for your handwriting of the transcript - he's from Chicago - you might explain. Do you use a computer to write the transcripts?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I transcribe the tape directly on to a Word document on computer, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. However, did you also have, and bring to Court with you, some brief handwritten notes regarding this incident on the 26th of March?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to offer the notes as a --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps you could read the notes into the record, Mr. O'Donnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps to make the record clear, we should give it a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Caution is necessary here. Do you have before you these notes with redaction or without?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the notes are in my official diary. The diary in front of me is not redacted. The material redacted does not relate to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This is true for both pages we have here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So from -- it's the same diary. Right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. I think it's enough for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. O'Donnell, you actually redacted the material and made the photocopies of your diary. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Would you like to have a photocopy with the redactions or do you feel competent reading from the original?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I don't need the redacted copy. I can read from the original. The entry starts: "Monday, 26 March, 2001. Handover of arrest documentation to Evidence Unit. IIF for tape of arrest, for transcript, and for copy of documentation with him at time of arrest. Copy to Suellen and copy to Mazhar Inayat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Who is, for the record, who did you are you referring to as Suellen? Who were you referring to

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Suellen is Suellen Taylor, and investigator with Team 1. The next segment is: "Black personal bag containing documentation of Stakic, Milomir, as per IIF re same of 25 March 2001, handed over to Mazhar Inayat 26 March, 2001." And Mr. Inayat has signed the receipt and dated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. O'Donnell, I believe at one point when counsel and the Court were going over documents, you were going over and looked through S220 through S226. Is that correct? Do you have those in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I recall in Court when we had the photocopies, one page was poorly copied, and the last digit of the ERN was not visible. I have a better copy of that page. I don't know if we could substitute that, which shows the full ERN number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It was one ending with 11?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't have it before me now. But before turning to this point, in order to have a systematic approach, can we please know who decided from these 81 photocopies to present especially these we have before us now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That was myself, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So you are in possession of all the 81?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, and the Defence also has all 81 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So once again, poor Judges, not having access to all the information. We have to live with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We would be happy to make it available but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I was going to ask the Court what time Your Honour plans to take a break because I am a concerned that you don't have a copy of this one page 211.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. That's correct. Please, before having the break, let's go into details, I am afraid this questionnaire has not yet a number. We waited for this because we didn't have an English translation, and we didn't have any questions from your side on this issue. Therefore, it remains with a number provisionally attached to these documents and the documents were, under these numbers, already admitted into evidence. And may then one tape be given to the Defence and one tape to the registry, please. What about the remaining two pages attached to these notes of arrest? I can't see any objections. So then they would be S232 and 233A. And it is necessary to have it under seal or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't think there's any information... Any additional problem? Sorry, now I made a mistake. The information index form had already 232, and therefore the attachments would be 233 and 234. I hope we have everything now in a correct order. And this allows to make a break. And the trial stays adjourned until 12.50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Thank you for this. Unfortunately, I didn't see in the transcript that indeed the questionnaire was already admitted into evidence. This has now the number, after re-numberation, 230-1. And then I learned that the OTP ex officio wants to provide us with the 81 documents, or copies better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. During our break, Ms. Karper was working and has several items for us. The 81 pages, we have three copies for the Trial Chamber. In addition, when it's convenient, we have the redacted version, and I must admit I'm a little confused now what the number is, the notes of arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's the questionnaire, isn't it, 231?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It becomes difficult today. We need to have some order in these flying documents, and therefore, even though I know that apparently the documents now before the witness are included in this set of documents, the 81 documents mentioned in the transcript already, they have to be admitted. I understand they are tendered. I understand the Defence is in possession of all these 81 photocopies. And therefore, the next available would be 235, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then let's please mark this entire bundle as S235, and then we don't do this -- won't do this exercise now, but page per page in the order as we have it, -1, -2, and following. Thank you. Mr. Koumjian, you may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just a few more questions and I believe I will be finished. Mr. O'Donnell, you reviewed S220 through S226. Is that correct? Did you have a chance to compare the ERN numbers on those documents to the range of numbers assigned by the Evidence Unit?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honours. The documents in front of me are marked with the ERN numbers, top right-hand corner. The ERN numbers are part of the range on the IIF form for the documents that I lodged with the Evidence Unit, those documents being the documents in the possession of Mr. Stakic at the time of his arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And does that, then, allow you to conclude that these are copies of the same documents that were in the black bag carried by Mr. Stakic on the plane the day of the arrest?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. These are documents that were taken by myself from Mr. Stakic, copies of which were lodged in the Evidence Unit with the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only other issue I have is S226. I believe that the copy that the Court had was the one that was missing the last digit. And somewhere before me, I have a -- Ms. Karper has better copies that have the entire range. Perhaps they could be substituted. It's also, of course, included in S235, that particular page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [No microphone]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just to explain a little, briefly, 235, this is the 81 pages of photocopies that you made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that there were things like cards that you put on one page, several cards, to photocopy together?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And did you photocopy an address book and each of the pages of the address book?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And did you photocopy a passport and at least several pages of the passport?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And the only other item is the IIF form, the information index form.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We have copies for all parties, now. I have no further questions on direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. O'Donnell.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You testified on direct that you're with the Office of the Prosecutor and that you're in the Team 1, and that you're an investigator. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. The investigation team leader of another team.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you just give me your specific title, if you would be kind enough to do so?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Investigations team leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As an investigations team leader, can you tell me what your background is? Is it criminal, is it something else?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, my background is criminal investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And how long, sir, have you been a criminal investigator?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: As I think I mentioned earlier, I joined the Australian federal police in 1982, so from that point onwards I have been involved in criminal investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me with this if you don't mind. Can you tell me why it is when you arrest an individual, as a criminal investigator, specifically Dr. Stakic, you would warn him of his right to remain silent, and then proceed to continue to engage him in conversations on no less than four occasions?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: There are certain things that have to be advised under the Rules of the Tribunal, Your Honours, when there's an arrest. I informed Mr. Stakic immediately that he didn't have to answer any questions. Out of fairness to him, I advised him of all of his rights, and also advised him of the procedure to be followed when he was to arrive in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, did Dr. Stakic at any time misunderstand specifically your caution and remark as follows, and it's reflected on page 2 of your report. Specifically, in the first third portion of the report, quote by you, Mr. O'Donnell, sir: "I have to advise you that you do not have to say anything. Anything that you say -- " "Anything that you do say will be recorded and may be used in evidence in any Tribunal proceedings, including a trial. Do you understand?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Objection to asking this witness what Mr. Stakic's understanding is. He can give Mr. Stakic's response, but he couldn't look into his mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. O'Donnell, was there ever an impression by you by Dr. Stakic that he did not understand your cautionary remarks with respect to having the right to remain silent?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, there was not. To the contrary, he specifically said that he understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then subsequent to that, following on the latter portion of that same page 2, sir, you tender to Dr. Stakic an arrest warrant, translated in B/C/S, correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Then you tell him, and in fact Dr. Stakic asks you whether or not he can read the arrest warrant, and you tell him he can read it later. Right?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is correct. I -- rather than just giving it to him, allowing him to read it and take it away, I actually left the warrant with him to read on the flight.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But sir, it's not a question of whether you left the warrant with him. He asked you: "May I read it?" You responded: "You can read it later." And then immediately thereafter, you started questioning him about the warrant that you knew and you instructed him to read at a later time. Isn't that what's reflected on the bottom portion of page 2 of this transcript?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's not quite correct. Immediately after handing him the B/C/S version of the arrest warrant, I also handed him a B/C/S version of his rights under Rules 42 and 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then you immediately asked him questions about the very arrest warrant that you, sir, told him that he could read at a later time. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: The question I asked him was whether the warrant related to him, and he obviously read his name and said it was his first and last names.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that, to you, was sufficient for you to reach the conclusion, by him reading simply his first and last name, that that was the individual that's contained in the warrant. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Not entirely, Your Honours. Mr. Stakic had been detained by local authorities. There was documentation relating to that detention that I signed at Belgrade airport at the time that he was handed over. Local authorities had detained him as the person in that arrest warrant. That, combined with him stating that it was his name, led me to believe that it was in relation to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you, Mr. O'Donnell, at any time make representations to Dr. Stakic which were not fulfilled by yourself?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. O'Donnell, look on page 4 of the transcript wherein you tell Dr. Stakic again, "You have a right to remain silent," in essence, and that "We will not, sir, have a conversation until you have a legal representative with you." Is that not a promise that you made to Dr. Stakic? And thereafter, ten minutes later, you once again engage him in conversation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That is correct. However, Your Honours, at the time, perhaps I should have stated it more clearly, that I was not going to question him Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French English transcripts in relation to the substance of the charges. Out of fairness to him, I still gave him information about what was to happen. And there was other conversation but not in relation to the charges. You will note that I advised him to inform the Detention Unit of his medical condition because he told me about that. There was other conversation, but clearly not in relation to the charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with the term or the use of the word "chain of custody"?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What is your understanding of it? I have a specific definition, but I'd rather use yours since you're the expert or professional in connection with these types of procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If that's asking for a legal definition, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, with respect to any evidence that is taken from a potential or a person who is indicted, would it be fair to say that the criminal practice here at the Tribunal, and in all the times that you worked as a criminal investigator, is to document and inventory a chain of custody for evidence. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That is correct. There should be a record made, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why should there be a record made, sir?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: The purpose of chain of custody is so that the steps in the chain of evidence coming from a certain location can be retraced. We know who has had possession of, in this case, documentation and what has happened to it in this case, being lodged in the Evidence Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to, sir, the evidence that usually is placed or the evidence that we're discussing could be weapons, and it could be also documentary evidence as you suggest. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, it's important to have this chain of custody, if you will, and the purpose of having it established properly and adequately is so that it would not distort the objective criminal proceedings that were going to take place. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I follow your question about distorting the objective criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me give you a hypothetical, if I may, and see if you can follow it. If, for example, a gun, a weapon, a piece of evidence, was used in a crime, and that gun was taken into the custody by a police officer, and subsequently the police officer left the gun at home, other people used the gun, grabbed the gun, took the gun to other places, returned it, would that piece of evidence have any credible weight in a court of law? Or would the chain of custody clearly have been broken or breached?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The answer has to be found by the Judges, not by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to the chain of custody and the documentation that you seized from Dr. Stakic, my first question to you is: Did you have a search and seizure subpoena to take his personal effects from him during his arrest?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, I did not, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Under what authority or law, sir, are you given the right to take the personal effects of any individual?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Objection, asking for a legal argument from the witness. The witness says he didn't have a warrant. The attorneys in the case, the Prosecution, with argue the legality under the Tribunal law of a seizure at the time of arrest of the items in possession of an individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's fair that we learn from the witness's point of view what was the legal basis for doing so, to find the legal answer once again is later for the Judges --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- only his subjective feeling, and that what the witness regarded as the legal basis. This may be of importance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the documentation in the bag of Mr. Stakic was searched by me for two reasons: One is to check what was in the bag, to ensure that there was nothing that could harm him or myself during the journey back to The Hague. As I mentioned, he was not restrained during that journey, apart from wearing a seat belt. The second was because he was under arrest, to see whether there was any material that may have evidential value on him at the time. In the jurisdiction that I come from, that's the general practice. My understanding here is that the Prosecutor, and through the Prosecutor, members of the Office of the Prosecutor have the right to do that generally under the powers of the Office of the Prosecutor, to investigate matters generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you, sir, advise Dr. Stakic about the fact that you were seizing documents from him and that those documents may be used in evidence against him, the same caution or similar caution that you gave him with his right to remain silent? Did you give him that instruction, sir?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, no, I did not. The seizure of documents was not something that he had an option in. And so it wasn't something that he could decline.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to the safety issue that you raise for the purposes of examining the black bag that was in the possession of Dr. Stakic, would it be a reasonable assumption, sir, to make that you searched that bag immediately, or would it be fair, based on the transcript that you -- the transcript that you gave us, you weren't concerned about safety; it was a small bag. And you only searched the bag, sir, after one hour and 45 minutes having been with Dr. Stakic. Namely, I reference page 4 and the time at 5.40, taking off from Belgrade, and the paragraph immediately below, suggesting that you searched the bag.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wasn't overly concerned about safety to the point that I had to search him immediately. The reason for that was he had already been searched before boarding the plane. That should have been good enough. However, to satisfy myself, that was a matter that I took into consideration in searching the bag, but the second matter was to see whether there was any material of evidentiary value.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Going back to this chain of custody and documents and evidence that can be utilised in criminal proceedings, sir, is it fair to say that when you're seizing certain documents, a professional such as yourself should in fact make a complete and detailed inventory of the materials that you seize from an individual who is indicted?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is not practicable in all situations. In the situation here, there was a large amount of documentation. The documentation was in Serbian. And to be able to itemise that material, I would have had to have some sort of summary of each of the documents. So it simply was not practicable for that to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you have an interpreter there on the plane with you that was assisting you in translating the conversations between you and Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would that individual have been a practical person you could have asked if you had any questions about identifying the documents?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That is the case. However, for the volume of material, the number of documents that were with Mr. Stakic at the time, it would not have been practicable to get a summary translation of all of those in the time available.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting, Mr. O'Donnell, that you translate verbatim each and everything that's listed, but to catalogue or to inventory the documents, do you think that it would have taken a significant amount of time, or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I do believe that it would have taken a significant amount of time, Your Honours, and longer than we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, that one of documents that you seized from Dr. Stakic was an address book, and in fact the majority, in essence, 70 pages of the documents that you seized, were merely an address book which contained telephone numbers and names of individuals such as his friends, neighbours, relatives, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do recall that there was an address book. As to the contents, I cannot comment because there was not time to go through that in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, Mr. O'Donnell, if I'm correct that approximately 70 of those 81 pages that you seized of the documentary evidence from Dr. Stakic was an address book, would you agree with me that the remaining 8 to 11 pages would have been rather straightforward and simple to inventory by yourself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can't see any longer the relevance of your question. Sorry for this. You made the point, and you asked a legal question. You'll get the answer by the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. O'Donnell, can you tell me what this IIF form is, the information index form?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: The information index form is filled out prior to lodging evidence with the Evidence Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And who would prepare that report, sir?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: The report was prepared by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And in that report, sir, do you note that they actually request and require there to be a response to a question relating to chain of custody, whether it was followed or not? Correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I agree that the words "chain of custody" are written on the form.
