utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that after the words "chain of custody," there's a response that's typed in, presumably by you, that states "no"?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's correct. That relates to how the documents should be treated by the Evidence Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So explain to me what this means when there's an indication "chain of custody" and your response "no."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: There are two issues here. The first is whether documents are chain of custody. The second is whether the documents should be treated as chain of custody when they are taken over by the Evidence Unit. Whether we have chain of custody on documents up to the time that they are delivered to the Evidence Unit depends on, obviously, the handling of those documents to that point, any statements and other things that we have showing the chain of custody. With certain documents, we may request that the Evidence Unit treat those as chain of custody because they may have to be signed in and out, for example, documents that have been taken to the forensic lab for handwriting analysis, perhaps photographs and other things. When that occurs, when there's a chain of custody form -- sorry, when it's marked "yes," a chain of custody form is generated so then as it's signed in and out of the evidence unit, it's treated in accordance with chain of custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So in fact, sir, on this IIF form where you identify the type of evidence it is, namely, document, the language that the document is written in, namely, B/C/S, I note that you have a document date that seems to be in error of 1899, December 30th.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's correct. Because there were, as it says, various documents and, obviously, various dates. Therefore, the number 1899 is put down so that there's no confusion that it could be -- if we pick an arbitrary date that was 1992, someone might think that it was, in fact, 1992. So we pick a date that is outside the range of probability.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So are you referencing in that section -- I don't think I understand that. But are you referencing in that section the documents that you seized? Correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So within that section, since you're referencing the documents that you seized, do you see when you identify those documents that in fact you state that documents were not signed? Correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you, sir -- can you explain to us why you did not fill out in the centre portion of this IIF form the rest of the material that was requested, such as location, source reference, date from victim details, witness details, date to, and perpetrator details?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Certainly. Your Honours, where individual documents are given an information index form, in other words, where there is one of these forms for a specific document, I would indicate whether that document is signed or not and give other details relevant to that document. In this case, various documents were put into the Evidence Unit. Some of those documents were signed. Others were business cards, general records. There would have been different dates and, therefore, that information is generic. Therefore, there's no details recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, sir, if you can tell me why, if the arrest of Dr. Stakic occurred on the 23rd of March, 2001, is it fair to say that you would have immediately, as a criminal investigator, proceeded to hand those documents over and to complete this IIF form as required by your very own Office of the Prosecution policy and procedures? Why did it take you, sir, two days to complete a simple task of filling this form out in part?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Well, partly for the reason that those two days were the weekend, and the Evidence Unit is not open on the weekend. But also, there had to be a transcript prepared, and that was lodged also.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is this form, sir, that you have also a form that's within your computer database?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So this is a form, sir, that you could have filled out immediately upon your arrival here at The Hague here in the Netherlands upon your release of Dr. Stakic to The Hague authorities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The witness could, but evidently he didn't, for the reasons given, and I can't see the relevance of a delay of two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, I have one question, if I may, one last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. O'Donnell, with respect to the chain of custody of documents, what length of time, sir, do you think is significant that a chain of custody for such evidentiary materials would be constituted a breach or considered a breach?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It depends entirely on the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you give us a range or it would just depend on each and every circumstance?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It depends entirely on the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just for purposes of clarification. We touched upon this issue already earlier during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you, Mr. O'Donnell, please tell us who decided to make photocopies instead of having the originals together?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I decided that, Your Honour. Perhaps if I can explain. At the time of taking possession of this documentation, the documents firstly were in Serbian. Secondly, I'm not involved in this investigation. I'm the investigation's team leader of another team involved in different investigations. Therefore, I was not in the best position to make an assessment of what would be relevant and what would not be relevant to the investigation. However, in case there was something of relevance, the documents were photocopied, lodged into evidence, and the original documents were handed over to the team responsible to be given back. At the time, the documents appeared to be various financial records - again, without translating, it was difficult to say exactly what was there - and identification documents. So there was nothing that appeared immediately as being very important evidentiary -- evidentially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To whom in person did you give the originals?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: The bag containing all of the original documentation was passed on to Mr. Inayat from Team 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So all the documents we have before us now in the form of a photocopy were given to Mr. Inayat for an assessment whether or not they would be necessary or could serve, maybe, as evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, they were given to Mr. Inayat. My understanding was that they would be returned. As I said, it was general identification documents, financial records, and so forth, which did not appear immediately to be of any great value to us. But the originals were handed over to Team 1 and the photocopies lodged with Evidence in case there was anything subsequently that was of interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You yourself mentioned beforehand the question whether or not a writing examination would be necessary or not. And it's not for us to decide on your decision or Mr. Inayat's decision, it's only for us to find out what was the order, what happened in your sphere, and my understanding is that you gave the originals to Mr. Inayat, a witness we hear later. But just for final clarification, before filling out the information index form, it was necessary for you to give to each document the registration number we can find on these pages now. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's not correct, Your Honour. Before handing the documents to the Evidence Unit, it was necessary for me to complete the information index form. That number has -- sorry, that form has the details of the documents and a number. I then hand that form, along with the documents to the Evidence Unit. The documents are individually assigned a reference number by the Evidence Unit. And after that, that number is assigned, the range is then put on to the information index form and appears at the centre top of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This centre part was only later filled in?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. After the documents are assigned a registration number, the Evidence Unit who assign that number then put that number on to this form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And this happened when? Was it still in your sphere?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I handed the documents to the Evidence Unit on Monday, the 26th of March, 2001. And that process took place after that. But the process was done by the Evidence Unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: My question was only, during cross-examination you said that you yourself on a computer document filled in this index form. The question is now: Evidently, you couldn't or were not able to finalise this work because you hadn't those numbers.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I filled out the details. The numbers are then assigned by the Evidence Unit, and then the form cannot be changed by me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. No other questions. Any other questions by the parties? No, it's not the case. Thank you for assisting us immediately. And we know better now about how the documents came into the possession of the OTP. And we thank you for coming immediately and giving us this detailed information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the usher escort the witness out of the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we turn immediately to the comments given by the Defence as regards the fourth notice, 92 bis statements tendered by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe upon reflection and consultation, we believe that the witness should be brought viva voce as he was initially offered. However, I'm somewhat confused as to the bases that the Office of the Prosecutor is citing for witnesses being brought under 92 bis. Simply to suggest, and I say it most respectfully to my learned friend, that it is a "crime witness" would lead us to, at times, feel that some of the witnesses that did, such as the witness that appeared yesterday and the day before, who were actually fact witnesses who dealt specifically with some of the atrocities that they have personally sustained and allege, clearly indicated they didn't know Dr. Stakic, never met Dr. Stakic, never heard of Dr. Stakic. During both questioning, I think by the OTP, the Defence, and the Honourable Court, those classically can be identified also as crime witnesses, yet they were brought in. We believe, for purposes that we are still reviewing and hope to examine, that the witness offered by the OTP should be called, as they initially suggested, live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any observations in response to both the fourth and the fifth notice?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had asked earlier today if the Defence was going to make an objection, and I thought they indicated no. That's why I'm not prepared to talk about the substance of this statement. But in answer to the question regarding how we choose these witnesses, we follow the factors outlined in Rule 92 bis. First of all, if a witness is going to testify to the conduct of the accused, we do not believe he's eligible for submission of a transcript. If the witness is only testifying to, for example, being a victim of crime, crime-base type evidence, again we've adopted the practice in this case of trying to present the major crimes that were committed, at least through one live witness, but to avoid repetition of evidence by having witnesses come in and testify to the same crime. I think the rule is clear as to what the Court will look at. It's discretionary with the Trial Chamber. The rule is clear that the Trial Chamber can consider various factors in deciding whether or not the witness should testify live. And I have not heard a reason given by the Defence about why the -- bringing this witness to testify viva voce would assist Your Honours in reaching an ultimate conclusion in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, I can clarify a point, if you would merely indulge me. I did have a conference with my learned friend during the break in connection with this, and I apologise to the Court and to him. His request on the fourth notice for admission of transcripts and videos pursuant to Rule 92 bis has now been put before me. Specifically with respect to that witness, Your Honour, identified under 65 ter number 41, as counsel and I discussed specifically the name of that individual, we do not have an objection. My comments specifically, Your Honour, were addressed to a witness under 65 ter number 40, which was previously -- which is the fifth witness under initial calling order, which was given and permitted to be submitted under 92 bis and given the pseudonym "F," I believe. We specifically would like to have --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I could short-circuit it. That witness is listed now as a live witness. I think there's some confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: There obviously is. Thank you. Judge, so with respect to the fourth notice, we do not have an objection, and that witness, with the Court's permission, can be submitted pursuant to Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So in conclusion, I'm happy to hear the contributions. We can expect Witness Number 40 appearing as a live witness. And as regards the other witnesses and statements, documents provided in the fourth and fifth notice, there are no objections to admit this under 92 bis. It's only number 40, and number 40 appears live. Right? Thank you. Then this seems to be clear. In order to avoid problems on Monday, my understanding is that on Monday, we have a witness where the problem may arise of having the lineup. And may I hear whether or not the parties agreed, (a) on a photo board; (b) on persons to be presented for this line-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We have not agreed on -- the persons have not all been gathered at one place or at one time. And I just received information I wanted to bring up one matter with Your Honour. One of the volunteers has indicated just to me in a phone call this morning a reluctance because this witness is from the Former Yugoslavia, if his face will be on television. He does feel concerned about his safety or reputation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think this can be resolved in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, I don't have a problem with at least the participants in the line-up not being on television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But I think one practical question, correct me if it's not such one, I think it would be only correct that the witness is in the courtroom before Dr. Stakic and the other persons enter the courtroom, which causes one problem. Dr. Stakic has, of course, the right to be present in the courtroom. It would facilitate the proceedings from my point of view if Dr. Stakic would waive, in consultation with the Defence counsel, of course, this right to be present immediately in the beginning of this hearing - we'll say just for the purposes of taking the solemn declaration - and then enter the courtroom together with the other persons. Would it be suitable for the Defence and for Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, briefly upon consultation with Dr. Stakic, we would waive at this time this limited right to be present while the witness is brought in and is given the oath to read, or the declaration to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This is also your own and personal declaration, Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with this, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Any other -- please be seated again. Any other practical problems in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Not at the present time, although it just occurred to me that if five individuals walk in together, the issue of security, I'm not sure how security wants to handle that. But they can deal with that. Perhaps these other issues may arise Monday afternoon. We'll just have to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But please, I don't want to make the experience on Monday afternoon that there is a practical problem that there's no agreement on the photo board and so on. Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: On the photo board, to be honest, I don't see how practically there would be any value, to be honest, to showing a photo board after the witness has just seen the person walk into court. We have the same photo board that was presented to the Defence earlier. They indicated they objected to 2 out of the 12 pictures. In my jurisdiction, normally we only show 6 to begin with. So they indicated that they thought 10 or 9 others were appropriate. At this point, I don't think -- we also did try to change the photo board, and we found it was not possible because Dr. Stakic's picture came out a completely different colour than the others. And it wasn't possible -- he would have stood out. It would not have been an Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French English transcripts appropriate photo board. I'm not sure of all the technical aspects of that. But I saw the attempt to make a new photo board, and it was much worse than the one that was previously shown. But to answer the question, we don't plan to show it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any other problems from the side of the Defence as regards this special procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Only with respect to, Your Honour, if my learned friend would give us at least some ample notice when we can examine from either a distance the participants that they are suggesting would take part in this identification. I know I've -- several of them were pointed out to me in passing, so I just would like to see the complete group of individuals to assess both their characteristics, such as their height, colour of hair, et cetera. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we shouldn't really do too much harm to these additional persons. And wouldn't it be a solution that, say, 15 minutes before starting of this hearing, you meet together and then decide spontaneously. Would it be possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That would be acceptable, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: One matter occurs to me for purposes of a record of this procedure, although we indicated the participants would not be -- their faces would not be broadcast, to have a record of the procedure, I think it would be necessary or very helpful to have some video done of the participants going in. I don't know if that can be arranged with the audiovisual unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No doubt, the Trial Chamber makes advantage of these possibilities, of course, and has done it also in the past already. And it's without any doubt that we ask the unit to concentrate first with one camera on the persons entering the courtroom and second on the witness. And this does not mean that it's in public, but as we said before, this entire exercise should be in closed session. I think the practical problems are resolved now. This concludes our today's hearing. And the trial stays adjourned until Monday, 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
